title: Experimental Chemistry
seo_title: Secondary 3 Chemistry: Experimental Chemistry Worksheets (O-Level 6092 with Answers)
standard_text: Name appropriate apparatus for measuring time, temperature, mass and volume, including burettes, pipettes, measuring cylinders and gas syringes; suggest methods of collecting gases based on their solubility and density and of drying them; describe methods of separation and purification (filtration, crystallisation, evaporation, simple and fractional distillation, use of a separating funnel, paper chromatography) and interpret chromatograms using Rf values and locating agents; deduce the purity of a substance from its melting or boiling point (summary of the Singapore-Cambridge O-Level Chemistry 6092 syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Secondary 3 O-Level Chemistry worksheets on experimental chemistry: measuring apparatus, collecting and drying gases, separation methods, chromatography, Rf values and purity. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Choose the method by the properties.
key_sub: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent.
body_html:
How to think about it

Choose apparatus and methods to suit the substances.

  • Accurate volumes: pipette (fixed volume) and burette (variable). Gas volume: gas syringe.
  • Gases: insoluble ones over water; soluble ones by downward delivery (denser than air) or upward delivery (less dense). Dry ammonia with calcium oxide, most other gases with concentrated sulfuric acid.
  • Separation: filtration (insoluble solid), crystallisation, evaporation, distillation, fractional distillation, separating funnel, paper chromatography.
  • A pure substance has a sharp, fixed melting point. Impurities lower the melting point (over a range) and raise the boiling point.
Example

Spot 4.2 cm, solvent 7.0 cm. Rf?

4.2 ÷ 7.0

Answer: 0.60

Example

How do you collect dry ammonia?

dry with calcium oxide

less dense than air, very soluble

Answer: upward delivery

Common mistakes

  • Using a measuring cylinder when an accurate volume is needed.
  • Collecting very soluble gases such as ammonia over water.
  • Heating copper(II) sulfate solution to dryness instead of crystallising it.
  • Dividing the solvent distance by the spot distance for Rf.

faq.q: How do you choose a method to collect a gas?
faq.a: If it is insoluble in water, collect it over water. If it is soluble, use downward delivery if it is denser than air or upward delivery if it is less dense.

faq.q: How do you calculate an Rf value?
faq.a: Divide the distance moved by the spot by the distance moved by the solvent front, both measured from the base line. Rf is always less than 1.

faq.q: How can you tell if a substance is pure?
faq.a: A pure substance melts and boils at fixed temperatures. Impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range of temperatures.

items.q: A burette reads 1.45 cm³ before a titration and 20.45 cm³ at the end point. What volume of acid was added?
items.e: Titre = final reading − initial reading = 20.45 − 1.45 = 19.00 cm³.

items.q: Which apparatus is best for measuring the volume of acid added drop by drop in a titration?
items.e: The volume of acid added drop by drop in a titration: a burette.

items.q: Which apparatus is best for measuring about 50 cm³ of water to dissolve a solid?
items.e: About 50 cm³ of water to dissolve a solid: a measuring cylinder.

items.q: Why must a gas be collected only after the air in the apparatus has been pushed out?
c: The gas is too hot at first.
The first gas is always poisonous.
Otherwise the first gas collected is mostly air.
items.e: Let the first bubbles escape.

items.q: A burette reads 0.10 cm³ before a titration and 22.85 cm³ at the end point. What volume of acid was added?
items.e: Titre = final reading − initial reading = 22.85 − 0.10 = 22.75 cm³.

items.q: A burette reads 1.55 cm³ before a titration and 25.50 cm³ at the end point. What volume of acid was added?
items.e: Titre = final reading − initial reading = 25.50 − 1.55 = 23.95 cm³.

items.q: Which apparatus is best for measuring the temperature change in a neutralisation?
items.e: The temperature change in a neutralisation: a thermometer.

items.q: A burette reads 1.65 cm³ before a titration and 23.30 cm³ at the end point. What volume of acid was added?
items.e: Titre = final reading − initial reading = 23.30 − 1.65 = 21.65 cm³.

items.q: Why is a gas syringe used to measure the volume of a gas?
c: It makes the gas react faster.
It changes the gas into a liquid.
It measures the volume of gas given off directly and accurately.
items.e: Readings can be taken at time intervals.

items.q: What is the residue in filtration?
c: the solid that stays on the filter paper
items.e: The liquid that passes through is the filtrate.

items.q: A burette reads 1.55 cm³ before a titration and 20.95 cm³ at the end point. What volume of acid was added?
items.e: Titre = final reading − initial reading = 20.95 − 1.55 = 19.40 cm³.

items.q: In fractional distillation of ethanol and water, which liquid distils first?
c: ethanol, because it has the lower boiling point (78 °C)
items.e: The fractionating column separates liquids with close boiling points.

items.q: Which apparatus is best for measuring exactly 25.0 cm³ of an alkali to put in a conical flask?
items.e: Exactly 25.0 cm³ of an alkali to put in a conical flask: a pipette.

items.q: A burette reads 0.80 cm³ before a titration and 23.10 cm³ at the end point. What volume of acid was added?
items.e: Titre = final reading − initial reading = 23.10 − 0.80 = 22.30 cm³.

items.q: Which apparatus is best for measuring the volume of gas given off every 10 s?
items.e: The volume of gas given off every 10 s: a gas syringe.

items.q: Which apparatus is best for measuring the mass of a sample of salt?
items.e: The mass of a sample of salt: an electronic balance.

items.q: Four titres are 23.65, 23.55, 24.80, 23.60 cm³. Using only the concordant results (within 0.10 cm³), what is the average titre?
items.e: Ignore the rough titre 24.80 cm³ and average the other three.

items.q: Colourless amino acids are separated by chromatography. How are their spots seen?
c: by looking at the paper in the dark
by spraying a locating agent (such as ninhydrin) and drying the paper
by heating the paper until it burns
items.e: The locating agent turns the spots coloured.

items.q: Four titres are 26.50, 25.25, 25.30, 25.35 cm³. Using only the concordant results (within 0.10 cm³), what is the average titre?
items.e: Ignore the rough titre 26.50 cm³ and average the other three.

items.q: How should you read the volume in a burette?
c: at eye level, from the bottom of the meniscus
only after the burette is empty
from the top of the meniscus
items.e: This avoids parallax error.

items.q: Why is carbon dioxide collected by downward delivery, or over water?
c: because it is very soluble in water and denser than air
because it is insoluble in water and less dense than air
because it is very soluble in water and less dense than air
because it is slightly soluble in water and denser than air
items.e: The method depends on solubility in water and density compared with air.

items.q: Which drying agent is commonly used for carbon dioxide?
items.e: Acidic or neutral gases are dried with concentrated sulfuric acid; calcium oxide would react with acidic gases.

items.q: Which drying agent is commonly used for sulfur dioxide?
items.e: Acidic or neutral gases are dried with concentrated sulfuric acid; calcium oxide would react with acidic gases.

items.q: Hydrogen is insoluble in water and less dense than air. How is it best collected?
c: in a gas syringe only, never in a test tube
items.e: Soluble gases cannot be collected over water. Gases denser than air: downward delivery; less dense: upward delivery.

items.q: Hydrogen chloride is very soluble in water and denser than air. How is it best collected?
items.e: Soluble gases cannot be collected over water. Gases denser than air: downward delivery; less dense: upward delivery.

items.q: Sulfur dioxide is soluble in water and denser than air. How is it best collected?
c: in a gas syringe only, never in a test tube
items.e: Soluble gases cannot be collected over water. Gases denser than air: downward delivery; less dense: upward delivery.

items.q: Which drying agent is used for ammonia?
items.e: Ammonia is alkaline, so it reacts with concentrated sulfuric acid (and with calcium chloride); calcium oxide is used.

items.q: Why is a pipette used instead of a measuring cylinder to measure 25.0 cm³ of solution in a titration?
c: A pipette is easier to clean.
A pipette measures a fixed volume much more accurately.
A measuring cylinder cannot measure 25 cm³.
items.e: Burettes and pipettes are precise to about 0.05–0.1 cm³.

items.q: Why is the base line in paper chromatography drawn in pencil, not ink?
c: Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent, so it will not run up the paper.
Pencil makes the spots move faster.
items.e: Ink would separate like the sample.

items.q: Why is a solution heated only until it is saturated, and then cooled, to make crystals of copper(II) sulfate?
c: Heating to dryness would drive off the water of crystallisation and decompose the crystals.
Cooling makes the solution more concentrated.
items.e: Crystals form as the saturated solution cools.

items.q: Chlorine is soluble in water and denser than air. How is it best collected?
items.e: Soluble gases cannot be collected over water. Gases denser than air: downward delivery; less dense: upward delivery.

items.q: Why is oxygen collected by over water (displacement of water)?
c: because it is very soluble in water and less dense than air
because it is very soluble in water and denser than air
because it is slightly soluble in water and denser than air
because it is insoluble in water
items.e: The method depends on solubility in water and density compared with air.

items.q: Why must the base line be above the solvent level in chromatography?
c: Otherwise the spots would dissolve into the solvent in the beaker.
items.e: The solvent must carry the spots up the paper.

items.q: Which drying agent is commonly used for chlorine?
items.e: Acidic or neutral gases are dried with concentrated sulfuric acid; calcium oxide would react with acidic gases.

items.q: Why is sulfur dioxide collected by downward delivery (upward displacement of air)?
c: because it is soluble in water and denser than air
because it is very soluble in water and less dense than air
because it is slightly soluble in water and denser than air
because it is insoluble in water and less dense than air
items.e: The method depends on solubility in water and density compared with air.

items.q: Which drying agent is commonly used for hydrogen?
items.e: Acidic or neutral gases are dried with concentrated sulfuric acid; calcium oxide would react with acidic gases.

items.q: Which drying agent is commonly used for hydrogen chloride?
items.e: Acidic or neutral gases are dried with concentrated sulfuric acid; calcium oxide would react with acidic gases.

items.q: Why is chlorine collected by downward delivery (upward displacement of air)?
c: because it is slightly soluble in water and denser than air
because it is very soluble in water and less dense than air
because it is soluble in water and denser than air
because it is insoluble in water and less dense than air
items.e: The method depends on solubility in water and density compared with air.

items.q: Oxygen is insoluble in water. How is it best collected?
items.e: Soluble gases cannot be collected over water. Gases denser than air: downward delivery; less dense: upward delivery.

items.q: Why is hydrogen collected by over water (displacement of water)?
c: because it is insoluble in water and less dense than air
because it is very soluble in water and denser than air
because it is slightly soluble in water and denser than air
because it is very soluble in water and less dense than air
items.e: The method depends on solubility in water and density compared with air.

items.q: Which separation technique works on this principle? Only magnetic materials such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are attracted to a magnet.
items.e: This is how magnetic attraction works.

items.q: What can be separated by simple distillation?
c: ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water
items.e: Pure water from seawater: simple distillation.

items.q: What can be separated by filtration?
c: the dyes in a sample of ink
ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water
items.e: Chalk (calcium carbonate) from water: filtration.

items.q: Which method is best for separating pure water from ink?
items.e: The water is collected as the distillate.

items.q: Which method is best for separating pure water from seawater?
items.e: Pure water from seawater: simple distillation.

items.q: Which method is best for separating pure water from orange juice?
items.e: Only the water boils off and is condensed.

items.q: Which method is best for separating ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water?
items.e: Ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water: fractional distillation.

items.q: Which method is best for separating nitrogen and oxygen from liquid air?
items.e: Nitrogen and oxygen from liquid air: fractional distillation.

items.q: Which method is best for separating chalk (calcium carbonate) from water?
items.e: Chalk (calcium carbonate) from water: filtration.

items.q: Which method is best for separating steel cans and aluminium cans at a recycling plant?
items.e: Steel is attracted to a magnet; aluminium is not.

items.q: Which method is best for separating sand and water?
items.e: Sand is insoluble, so it stays on the filter paper.

items.q: Which separation technique works on this principle? The solvent changes into a gas and escapes, leaving the dissolved solid behind.
items.e: This is how evaporation works.

items.q: What is the principle behind magnetic attraction?
c: The liquid with the lower boiling point boils first, and its vapour is cooled and condensed.
Different dyes have different solubilities in the solvent, so they travel different distances.
Only magnetic materials such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are attracted to a magnet.
The solvent changes into a gas and escapes, leaving the dissolved solid behind.
items.e: This is how magnetic attraction works.

items.q: Which method is best for separating salt from salt solution?
items.e: The water evaporates and leaves the salt behind.

items.q: Which method is best for separating sugar from sugar solution?
items.e: Heat gently: the solvent evaporates and the solute remains.

items.q: What can be separated by a separating funnel?
c: hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals from its solution
nitrogen and oxygen from liquid air
oil from a mixture of oil and water
items.e: Oil from a mixture of oil and water: a separating funnel.

items.q: What can be separated by filtration?
c: the dyes in a sample of ink
sand from a mixture of sand and water
oil from a mixture of oil and water
items.e: Sand from a mixture of sand and water: filtration.

items.q: What is the principle behind paper chromatography?
c: Different dyes have different solubilities in the solvent, so they travel different distances.
The liquid with the lower boiling point boils first, and its vapour is cooled and condensed.
The solvent changes into a gas and escapes, leaving the dissolved solid behind.
Insoluble solid particles are too big to pass through the tiny holes in the filter paper.
items.e: This is how paper chromatography works.

items.q: Which method is best for separating sand from a mixture of sand and water?
items.e: Sand from a mixture of sand and water: filtration.

items.q: Which method is best for separating the dyes in a sample of ink?
items.e: The dyes in a sample of ink: paper chromatography.

items.e: One spot (in all solvents) means pure; more than one means a mixture.

items.q: Pure salicylic acid melts at 159 °C. A sample of salicylic acid melts gradually from 153 °C to 157 °C. Is the sample pure?
items.e: Pure substances melt at one fixed temperature. Impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.

items.q: In paper chromatography, a spot moves 4.5 cm and the solvent front moves 10 cm from the base line. What is the Rf value?
items.e: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent = 4.5 ÷ 10 = 0.45.

items.q: In paper chromatography, a spot moves 3.6 cm and the solvent front moves 9 cm from the base line. What is the Rf value?
items.e: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent = 3.6 ÷ 9 = 0.4.

items.q: A dye has an Rf value of 0.3. The solvent front moves 12 cm. How far does the dye move?
items.e: Distance = Rf × solvent distance = 0.3 × 12 = 3.6 cm.

items.q: A spot moved 6 cm. The solvent moved 12 cm from the start line. What is the Rf value?
items.e: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent = 6 ÷ 12.

items.q: A white solid melts over a range from 115 °C to 119 °C. What can you conclude?
c: It contains an impurity, which lowers the melting point.
It contains a dissolved impurity, which raises the boiling point.
It is impure: impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.
It is a mixture of at least three dyes.
items.e: A white solid melts over a range from 115 °C to 119 °C.: It is impure: impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.

items.q: Pure ice melts at 0 °C. A sample of salty ice melts at −3 °C. What can you conclude?
c: It is probably pure benzoic acid.
It is a mixture of at least three dyes.
It contains a dissolved impurity, which raises the boiling point.
It contains an impurity, which lowers the melting point.
items.e: Pure ice melts at 0 °C. A sample of salty ice melts at −3 °C.: It contains an impurity, which lowers the melting point.

items.q: In paper chromatography, a spot moves 6 cm and the solvent front moves 8 cm from the base line. What is the Rf value?
items.e: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent = 6 ÷ 8 = 0.75.

items.q: A spot moved 3 cm. The solvent moved 10 cm from the start line. What is the Rf value?
items.e: Rf = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent = 3 ÷ 10.

items.q: A chromatogram of a food colouring shows one spot. What can you conclude?
c: It contains a dissolved impurity, which raises the boiling point.
It is probably pure benzoic acid.
It is impure: impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.
It may be a pure dye (one substance in that solvent).
items.e: A chromatogram of a food colouring shows one spot.: It may be a pure dye (one substance in that solvent).

items.q: In paper chromatography, a spot moves 6.4 cm and the solvent front moves 8 cm from the base line. What is the Rf value?
items.e: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent = 6.4 ÷ 8 = 0.8.

items.q: Pure aspirin melts at 136 °C. A sample of aspirin melts at exactly 136 °C. Is the sample pure?
items.e: Pure substances melt at one fixed temperature. Impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.

items.q: Pure naphthalene melts at 80 °C. A sample of naphthalene melts gradually from 74 °C to 78 °C. Is the sample pure?
items.e: Pure substances melt at one fixed temperature. Impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.

items.q: In paper chromatography, a spot moves 7.5 cm and the solvent front moves 10 cm from the base line. What is the Rf value?
items.e: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent = 7.5 ÷ 10 = 0.75.

It was compared with inks A, B and C. Which inks are in X?
items.e: Spots at the same height are the same dye.

items.q: A white solid melts sharply at 122 °C, the same as pure benzoic acid. What can you conclude?
c: It contains an impurity, which lowers the melting point.
It is impure: impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.
It contains a dissolved impurity, which raises the boiling point.
It is probably pure benzoic acid.
items.e: A white solid melts sharply at 122 °C, the same as pure benzoic acid.: It is probably pure benzoic acid.

items.q: Pure water boils at 100 °C at sea level. A sample boils at 102 °C. What can you conclude?
c: It is impure: impurities lower the melting point and make it melt over a range.
It contains an impurity, which lowers the melting point.
It contains a dissolved impurity, which raises the boiling point.
It may be a pure dye (one substance in that solvent).
items.e: Pure water boils at 100 °C at sea level. A sample boils at 102 °C.: It contains a dissolved impurity, which raises the boiling point.

items.q: Why is chromatography used in forensic science?
c: to measure the mass of evidence
to compare inks or dyes found at a crime scene with known samples
items.e: Matching spots suggest the same ink.

items.q: A dye has an Rf value of 0.2. The solvent front moves 10 cm. How far does the dye move?
items.e: Distance = Rf × solvent distance = 0.2 × 10 = 2 cm.

items.q: What can be separated by evaporation to dryness?
c: ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water
nitrogen and oxygen from liquid air
items.e: Salt from salt solution: evaporation to dryness.

items.q: Why must a liquid in a separating funnel be immiscible for the method to work?
c: The tap only opens for oils.
Immiscible liquids form separate layers, so the lower layer can be run off.
items.e: Oil and water are immiscible.

items.q: What can be separated by paper chromatography?
c: ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water
sand from a mixture of sand and water
the dyes in a sample of ink
items.e: The dyes in a sample of ink: paper chromatography.

items.q: A dye has an Rf value of 0.3. The solvent front moves 8 cm. How far does the dye move?
items.e: Distance = Rf × solvent distance = 0.3 × 8 = 2.4 cm.

items.q: Which is the best way to obtain pure water from a solution of ink?
items.e: Water boils off and is condensed; the dyes are left behind.

items.q: Why does cold water enter the condenser at the bottom?
c: so the condenser fills completely with water and cools the vapour efficiently
items.e: Counter-current cooling.

items.q: In paper chromatography, a spot moves 2 cm and the solvent front moves 8 cm from the base line. What is the Rf value?
items.e: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent = 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25.

items.q: A burette reads 1.60 cm³ before a titration and 26.95 cm³ at the end point. What volume of acid was added?
items.e: Titre = final reading − initial reading = 26.95 − 1.60 = 25.35 cm³.

items.q: Two dyes have the same Rf value in the same solvent. What does this suggest?
c: They may be the same substance.
items.e: Compare with known substances.

items.q: Why is hydrogen chloride collected by downward delivery (upward displacement of air)?
c: because it is insoluble in water and less dense than air

because it is slightly soluble in water and denser than air
because it is very soluble in water and denser than air
items.e: The method depends on solubility in water and density compared with air.

items.q: What can be separated by crystallisation?

ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water
oil from a mixture of oil and water

items.q: A burette reads 0.95 cm³ before a titration and 18.95 cm³ at the end point. What volume of acid was added?
items.e: Titre = final reading − initial reading = 18.95 − 0.95 = 18.00 cm³.

items.q: Why is ammonia collected by upward delivery (downward displacement of air)?

items.q: A student needs pure dry sodium chloride from rock salt (salt with sand). Which order of steps is correct?
c: dissolve in water, filter, evaporate the filtrate

items.e: Ignore the rough titre 21.30 cm³ and average the other three.
